dok_rationale: Part (c) requires adjudicating two interpretations by coordinating the boxplot with the dotplot, distinguishing summaries from distribution features, and defending which display answers a decision question; no single calculation determines the response.
stem: The displays show practice-test times, in minutes, for 24 students. Two students interpret the boxplot.\par\smallskip \textbf{Omar:} ``Most students took about 32 minutes---the middle of the box.''\par \textbf{Nia:} ``A boxplot cannot tell us whether most students took about 32 minutes.''
first_take: Who do you trust more, Omar or Nia? Point to one feature in either display.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Read the median and the first and third quartiles from the boxplot. What percent of the times lie in the box from Q1 to Q3?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the dotplot in context: include the two clusters, the gap, and the isolated high value. State two features that the boxplot preserves.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Whose interpretation is better supported? Cite the dotplot feature that settles it. Explain what a boxplot can and cannot show here. A coach asks whether most students need more than 30 minutes: choose a display, and explain what the boxplot alone would lead the coach to believe.

answers.a: Median $=32$ min, Q1 $=24$ min, and Q3 $=40.5$ min. The box contains the middle $50\%$ of the times. The full five-number summary is $(22,24,32,40.5,55)$.
answers.b: Two clusters: 12 times from 22--26 min and 11 from 38--44 min; a 27--37 min gap; isolated 55 min. Ordered data: 22, 22, 23, 23, 24, 24, 24, 25, 25, 25, 26, 26, 38, 38, 39, 39, 40, 40, 41, 41, 42, 43, 44, 55. The boxplot preserves median 32, quartiles 24 and 40.5, and spread 22--55; it hides the clusters and gap.
answers.c: Nia. No dot is near 32; the median is halfway between 26 and 38 in the gap, so 32 is not a typical cluster time. A boxplot shows center, quartiles, spread, and flagged outliers but hides gaps, clusters, and modality. Use the dotplot: 12 times are above 30 and 12 below, in two groups. The boxplot alone suggests one continuous group around 32.

expectedElements.description: Chooses Nia and cites that the median of 32 lies in the dotplot's 27--37 minute gap, with no observations nearby
Explains that the boxplot preserves center and spread but not the clusters, gap, or modality
Chooses the dotplot for the more-than-30-minute decision and uses the two groups or 12-of-24 split to justify it
Explains that the boxplot alone can make the data look like one continuous group centered near 32

scoringGuide.E: Chooses Nia, cites the empty interval around the median, accurately contrasts what the displays retain, and chooses the dotplot for the coach with the 12-of-24 split and the boxplot's misleading continuous-pile impression explained.
scoringGuide.P: Chooses Nia and cites the gap but gives only a general display comparison, OR chooses the dotplot with no count or consequence, OR provides the capabilities and consequence but never commits to an interpretation.
scoringGuide.I: Chooses Omar because 32 is the median, claims a boxplot shows the two clusters, or chooses a display with no feature from the data.

commonMistakes: Treating the median as the most common value; no student took 32 minutes
Calling the empty 27--37 interval a short bar even though the display is a dotplot
Saying a boxplot shows every observation because it shows the minimum and maximum
Calling 55 a formal $1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}$ outlier; the upper fence is $65.25$
Choosing the boxplot for the coach merely because it is more compact
